summary: Registers .onion as a Special-Use Domain Name. It is the name space used for services reached over Tor, so ordinary DNS should not try to resolve it.

plainLanguage.summary: Some web addresses end in .onion and only work through a special private network, so the regular address book should not look for them.

questions: why is .onion a special-use domain name
why can't dns resolve onion addresses
what does rfc 7686 require of dns servers
subtitle: Reserves .onion as a special name that belongs to Tor services and must never be resolved through ordinary DNS.

tldr.problem: Names ending in .onion are used to reach services over the Tor network, but ordinary DNS software does not know this and might try to look them up, which leaks information and cannot work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers .onion in the Special-Use Domain Names registry and says what each party (applications, resolvers, DNS servers, operators, registrars) MUST or SHOULD do when it sees such a name.
tldr.outcome: Only Tor-aware software handles .onion names; everyone else returns an error or NXDOMAIN, and nobody can register one.

today: RFC 7686 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the registration of .onion as a Special-Use Domain Name.

sections.title: What .onion Names Are
sections.content:
The Tor network can host network services under the .onion Special-Use Top-Level Domain Name. These names can be used like other domain names, for example in URLs (RFC 3986), but they do not use the DNS infrastructure. Instead, a .onion name corresponds to the identity of a service, so it combines location and authentication.

Services behind .onion names are end to end encrypted and anonymized. The identity and location of the server are obscured from the client, and the location of the client is obscured from the server. The client's identity may or may not be disclosed through an optional cryptographic authentication process.
sections.plainLanguage: A .onion address is like a secret clubhouse name. It tells you who the clubhouse is, not where the street is, and neither side learns where the other lives.

sections.title: Self-Authenticating Names Nobody Owns
sections.content:
.onion names are self-authenticating: they are derived from the cryptographic keys the server uses, in a way the client can verify while the connection is being established. For that reason the cryptographic label is not meant to be human-meaningful.

The Tor network is designed to have no central controlling authority for routing and service publication, so .onion names cannot be registered, assigned, transferred or revoked. "Ownership" comes solely from controlling the public/private key pair that matches the algorithmic derivation of the name.

Like other top-level names, .onion names can have any number of subdomain components. Tor itself does not use them, but application protocols such as HTTP (RFC 7230) can. The names must still conform to DNS name syntax, since they will still be exposed to DNS implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Your .onion name comes from your secret key, like a name tag that only your own key can prove. No office hands out names, so nobody can take yours away.

sections.title: What Each Party Must Do
sections.content:
The name is "special" in the sense of RFC 6761, because software has to treat it differently. Section 2 of the RFC lists the effects on seven kinds of parties:

  • Users are expected to know that .onion names have different security properties and work only through software that is aware of them.
  • Applications that implement Tor MUST recognize .onion names, either directly or through a proxy such as SOCKS (RFC 1928). Applications that do not implement Tor SHOULD generate an error and SHOULD NOT perform a DNS lookup.
  • Resolver libraries MUST either resolve the name according to the Tor rendezvous specification or answer NXDOMAIN.
  • Caching DNS servers not adapted for Tor SHOULD NOT look up .onion names and MUST generate NXDOMAIN for such queries.
  • Authoritative DNS servers MUST answer NXDOMAIN for .onion.
  • DNS server operators MUST NOT configure an authoritative server to answer for .onion.
  • Registries and registrars MUST NOT register .onion names, and all such requests MUST be denied.

The ban on registration does not stop IANA from putting a record in the root zone database to reserve the name, and it does not stop non-DNS providers such as trust providers from supporting .onion names.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who runs an address book is told: if someone asks for a .onion name, say "not here" and do not go hunting. Only the special secret-club software may answer.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content: The only IANA action is to register .onion in the registry of Special-Use Domain Names defined by RFC 6761. The registration template is the list of effects in Section 2 of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds .onion to the official list of reserved names so everybody knows it is a special one.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
The security properties of .onion names can be compromised if the server leaks its identity in another way (for example in an application-level message), if the access protocol is implemented or deployed incorrectly, or if the protocol itself has a flaw.

Look-alike names. Because .onion labels are not human-meaningful, an attacker may find keys that give names that look or read similar to the one the user wants. Mitigations are generating human-meaningful .onion names (at considerable computing expense) or following links from bookmarks and other trusted stores. Depending on the function used to build the label, an attacker may also find a key that collides with the same name with substantially less work than attacking the full-strength key, and could then impersonate the service.

Suffix confusion. Users need to understand the difference between example.onion and example.onion.tld, where .onion is only a subdomain of another name.

DNS leaks. A legacy client might try to resolve a .onion name through DNS. That discloses that the client is trying to reach a specific service over Tor, and malicious resolvers could record such leaks. The risk is reduced if client software no longer leaks such queries or supports Tor rendezvous, or if DNS software drops requests for .onion.
sections.plainLanguage: Two dangers: someone could make a fake name that looks almost the same as the real one, and an old program might shout the secret name to the regular address book. Saving bookmarks and updating software help.
